sentences.text: Harpactognathus was an exceptionally large rhamphorhynchid pterosaur, estimated to have a wingspan of at least 2.5 meters and a skull length between 280 and 300 millimeters.
Its most striking feature was an extremely broad snout that was wider than it was tall, containing four pairs of teeth for a total of at least 12.

A humerus assigned to the genus measures 110.5 millimeters in length, making it one of the largest known pre-Cretaceous pterosaur humeri, while a low bony crest ran along the snout to the tip of the beak.
Harpactognathus is exceptionally large for a rhamphorhynchid, with an estimated wingspan of at least 2.5 meters.
The animal possessed an extremely broad snout that was wider than it was tall in life, a trait not found in many other rhamphorhynchids.
A humerus assigned to Harpactognathus measures 110.5 mm in length, making it one of the largest known pre-Cretaceous pterosaur humeri.
The only confirmed fossil of Harpactognathus is an incomplete rostrum found in 1996 at the Bone Cabin Quarry in Albany, Wyoming.

Kenneth Carpenter and colleagues formally named the new genus and species Harpactognathus gentryii in 2003, and the species name honors Joe Gentry, a volunteer for the Western Paleontological Laboratories.
A pterosaur mandible was discovered in 1999 within a meter of the original rostrum find.

Based on its teeth and environment, Harpactognathus was likely a terrestrial carnivore living near freshwater, unlike its piscivorous relatives, and recent publications suggest scaphognathines like Harpactognathus likely lacked specializations for eating fish and were probably terrestrial predators of small vertebrates or generalists.
As a rhamphorhynchid, Harpactognathus may have been an aerial predator of small prey.

A premaxillary crest on the skull may have been supported by soft tissues for sexual display or represented sexual dimorphism, and Carpenter et al. (2003) presumed the function of the crest was for display purposes.

Harpactognathus belongs to the family Rhamphorhynchidae, but its exact position within that family remains debated, and it was originally classified in the subfamily Scaphognathinae within the family Rhamphorhynchidae.

Harpactognathus cannot be classified as a campylognathid because its tooth count and tooth socket anatomy do not match that group, and it was originally placed in the subfamily Scaphognathinae due to its widely spaced teeth.

Some researchers suggest Harpactognathus belongs to the subfamily Rhamphorhynchinae rather than Scaphognathinae based on similarities to Sericipterus and Angustinaripterus, and a 2010 phylogenetic analysis by Andres, Clark, and Xu placed Harpactognathus in the subfamily Rhamphorhynchinae as a close relative of Angustinaripterus and Sericipterus.

Many traits once considered unique to Harpactognathus are now recognized as also belonging to Sericipterus and/or Angustinaripterus, and it is debated whether Harpactognathus belongs to the tribe Angustinaripterini, as it was excluded from a 2022 analysis due to the fragmentary nature of the fossil.

Harpactognathus lived during the Late Jurassic period in the Morrison Formation of Albany County, Wyoming, USA, specifically in the Salt Wash Member during the Kimmeridgian stage, with a time range from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian (152.21 to 145.06 million years ago).
It is debated whether the mandible found near the holotype actually belongs to Harpactognathus due to its slender nature and alveoli anatomy.
